analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2001 Bush tax cuts permanent by removing their expiration dates.
analysis.headline: The bill to make the 2001 tax cuts permanent drew 88 cosponsors but never got a hearing or a vote, dying in the Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2001 tax law (EGTRRA) was written with expiration dates so it could pass under Senate budget rules. This bill would have struck the section containing those expiration dates, making every provision permanent: the income tax rate cuts, the phaseout of the estate tax, the expanded child tax credit, marriage penalty relief, education savings accounts, and other tax benefits. The bill never left the House Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: The largest dollar benefits of the 2001 law went to households at the top of the income scale, and repealing the estate tax entirely benefits only the largest estates. Middle-income families also gained from the expanded child credit, the 10% bracket, and marriage penalty relief, but on a much smaller scale per family. Permanent status would have locked in those top-rate and estate-tax benefits rather than letting them lapse as scheduled.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Title IX of the 2001 tax law, which contains the sunset provisions that would have terminated all of that law's tax benefits, making them permanent instead [S2][S3].

The provisions it locks in include cuts to income tax rates, the phaseout and repeal of the estate tax, expansion of the child tax credit, marriage penalty relief, education savings accounts, and earned income tax credit changes, as reflected in the bill's subject matter [S1].

analysis.who_pays: Making the tax cuts permanent would have reduced federal revenue permanently, meaning less money available for government spending or larger deficits. Because the bulk of the 2001 law's dollar value went to high earners and the estate tax repeal went exclusively to very large estates, the tax code would have become less progressive on a permanent basis.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal revenue and future government programs

drawbacks.text: The 2001 law's sunsets were not arbitrary: they existed so the tax cuts could fit within Senate budget rules, and their cost beyond the ten-year window was the reason. Making them permanent would have added roughly hundreds of billions of dollars per decade to the deficit, borne eventually by taxpayers through lower services or higher future taxes (general knowledge about why EGTRRA used sunsets).

The benefit is heavily skewed: estate tax repeal under the 2001 law applied only to estates above multimillion-dollar exemptions, and the rate cuts favored top brackets, while an honest supporter would acknowledge that the middle-class pieces (child credit, 10% bracket) were repeatedly extended on their own anyway.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill contains real benefits for middle-income families, but its dominant dollar effect is locking in tax cuts whose largest share goes to high-income households and the largest estates, with no offsetting revenue. The sunset dates it removes were the budget discipline mechanism that made the original law passable; striking them without any pay-for converts a temporary tax cut into a permanent structural deficit that weighs on working families through reduced public investment and future fiscal pressure.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the tax-writing committee, which never took it up, and it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Kenny Hulshof introduced the bill on April 3, 2003, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S5].
The bill attracted 88 cosponsors, 87 Republicans and 1 Democrat [S4].
The complete action history shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action beyond the referral; the bill died in committee when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained directly from the bill dying, but the federal Treasury was spared a permanent revenue commitment whose largest benefits flowed to top earners and large estates, and the concentrated interests behind the bill got nothing from this vehicle.

for.name: Rep. Kenny Hulshof
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the 2001 tax law's sunset provisions and referred it to Ways and Means.

for.name: 87 of 229 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill to make the 2001 tax cuts permanent.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a markup or a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: Of the 88 cosponsors, 87 were Republicans and 1 was a Democrat; the bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call to measure party positions.

industries.note: The bill would have permanently extended the top income tax rate cuts and estate tax repeal from the 2001 law, whose dollar value concentrated at the top of the income scale. Its death left the scheduled expirations intact for this vehicle, though Congress addressed parts of the same law in later bills.

industries.industry: Education savings and retirement account providers
industries.note: Permanent status for education savings accounts and IRA provisions would have given banks and fund managers a stable, long-term product line serving savers. The effect on ordinary savers is genuinely favorable, making this an aligned interest.
